label: conj:confinement-phase-boundaries
title: Phase boundaries of the confinement locus
html:
Let P be a confined particle, with confinement locus \Omega(P), active support \mathcal{S}^*(P, q), binding multiplicity \mu(P, q) and Frobenius stability index \sigma_F(P, q) as in 14.2.17. Let \mathcal{G} \subset \mathbb{R}_{>1} be the generic locus of q, and call a connected component \Omega_\alpha of \Omega(P) a confinement phase. Then:

  1. Stratification. The complement \mathcal{G} \setminus \Omega(P) is a real-algebraic stratification with strata of codimension \ge 1, the phase boundaries of P. Each stratum is the zero locus of a principal minor of the SDP Gram matrix.
  2. Strict complementarity on phases. On each phase \Omega_\alpha the SDP dual pair is continuous and strictly complementary, so the active support and \mu are constant on \Omega_\alpha by 14.2.17.
  3. Analyticity. \sigma_F(P, q) is real-analytic on each \Omega_\alpha.
  4. Scope. Level sufficiency, shell-closure stability and the Markov-trace preservation of the confinement category functor hold pointwise in each \Omega_\alpha and fail on \partial\Omega(P).
  5. Phase transitions. If a continuous path q: [0, 1] \to \mathcal{G} crosses a phase boundary at q_0 \in \partial\Omega(P), then at q_0 either P is not realisable as a closed-braid bound state (deconfinement), or \mu jumps, the active support gains or loses a Wedderburn block, and \sigma_F has a non-smooth point (regime switch), or both.

Supporting argument (not a proof). For (1): the entries of the Gram matrix are Laurent polynomials in q, so each principal minor that is not identically zero has finitely many real zeros in \mathcal{G}; what is not shown is that loss of strict feasibility happens exactly on these zero sets. For (2): strict complementarity holds for generic SDP data (Alizadeh–Haeberly–Overton), but genericity at the substrate parameters is not established. For (4): the proofs of 14.2.15 and 14.2.13 use a well-defined, locally constant active support. For (5): a boundary crossing is either a loss of strict primal feasibility or a dual variable u^*_\lambda passing through zero.
